beats.narration: Begin by framing Pipeline Foundations as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Consider this worked case: A self-driving car system defines the task as lane detection, uses grayscale intensity as representation, assumes consistent lighting, trains on labeled road images, and outputs a binary lane mask. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a four-panel diagram showing task definition, representation, assumptions, and decision rule, with arrows linking each stage to the next.

beats.narration: Now define Image Formation Basics precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Consider this worked case: A 3D building corner projects onto a 2D image plane, where perspective distortion is corrected using homography matrices derived from known camera parameters. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Image Formation Basics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a 3D cube with projected 2D coordinates, highlighting how perspective changes affect pixel mapping.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Appearance Modeling operates in a concrete sequence. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Consider this worked case: A matte white wall and a glossy white wall produce different pixel intensities under identical illumination, necessitating color-invariant features for reliable detection. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Appearance Modeling
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display side-by-side images of the same object under varying lighting and material conditions, with color histograms overlaid.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Motion Estimation and make the decision criteria explicit. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Consider this worked case: A video of a moving car is processed by comparing consecutive frames to calculate displacement vectors, enabling smooth trajectory prediction. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Motion Estimation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Animate a sequence of frames with tracked object paths overlaid, showing frame-to-frame comparison.

beats.narration: Apply Object Recognition to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Consider this worked case: A traffic sign image is analyzed by matching edge patterns and color distributions to a pre-trained classifier, outputting a 'stop' label with confidence score. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Object Recognition
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a traffic sign with bounding boxes, class labels, and confidence metrics, alongside a decision tree diagram.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Scene Understanding, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. Consider this worked case: A classroom image is parsed to identify desks, chairs, and students, with spatial relationships mapped to reconstruct room layout. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Scene Understanding
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a classroom scene with segmented regions, labeled objects, and a spatial relationship graph.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Image Representation with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Consider this worked case: A color photograph is converted to a 3D array of height, width, and channels, where each pixel value ranges from 0 to 255. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Image Representation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a color image with a numeric array overlay, highlighting channel separation and pixel value ranges.

beats.narration: Use Color Conversion to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Consider this worked case: An RGB image is transformed to HSV space to isolate green foliage from background noise, improving segmentation accuracy. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Color Conversion
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display RGB, HSV, and LAB color space versions of the same image, with channel separation visualized.

beats.narration: Connect Filtering and Feature Detection to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Consider this worked case: A blurred document image is sharpened using a Sobel filter, then analyzed with SIFT to extract keypoints for matching. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Filtering and Feature Detection
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a before/after image with filter kernels and detected feature points overlaid.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Consider this worked case: A face detection system is tested with rotated faces, different lighting, partial occlusion, and cross-database samples to measure accuracy drop. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist graphic with checkboxes for viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift, alongside performance metrics.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: An introduction to the underlying concepts of computer vision. The course will consider fundamental topics, including image formation, edge detection, texture analysis, color, segmentation, shape analysis, detection of objects in images and high level image representation. Depending on the interest of the class, more advanced topics will be covered, such as image database retrieval or robotic vision. Programming homework assignments that implement the concepts discussed in class are an integral part of the course. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-631. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

sources.author: OpenCV
sources.excerpt: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.
